blogs.title: The Staleness Trap: How *Farahi* Resolves the Tension Between Time and National Security in FOIA Litigation
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's handling of the 'passage of time' argument in Exemption 7(A) cases. While precedent like *CREW* warns against vague assertions that investigations are 'ongoing,' *Farahi* clarifies that a terse update declaration need not stand alone if it builds upon a previously detailed, albeit older, factual record. The article will explore how the court balanced the plaintiff's right to challenge stale claims against the practical realities of long-term counterterrorism investigations, effectively creating a 'supplemental update' doctrine for national security FOIA cases.

blogs.title: Information vs. Words: The Evolving Standard for Segregability in High-Volume Intelligence Files
blogs.description: Focusing on Part V of the opinion, this post examines the court's rigorous application of the segregability requirement when non-exempt material is 'interspersed line-by-line' within classified documents. By reaffirming that FOIA protects 'information, not simply words,' the *Farahi* decision offers critical guidance for agencies managing massive files (10,000+ pages) where redaction might render the remaining text meaningless or misleading. The analysis will discuss the implications for future litigation where plaintiffs argue that the sheer volume of responsive records statistically guarantees some releasable content.

blogs.title: The Adversarial Deficit: Procedural Fairness and the Reliance on Ex Parte Declarations in National Security FOIA
blogs.description: This post critiques the procedural mechanics of the *Farahi* ruling, specifically the heavy reliance on ex parte, under-seal declarations to resolve both the exemption applicability and segregability issues. With the appellant having forfeited certain arguments by failing to oppose the ex parte process earlier, the case highlights a growing trend where national security concerns effectively nullify the adversarial testing of evidence. The article will debate whether this procedural shortcut is an unavoidable necessity in terrorism-related cases or a dangerous erosion of due process rights for FOIA requesters.
